title: Tibetan Ice May Preserve the Last Ice Age
paragraphs: A team led by Ohio State University reports that an ice cap in northwest Tibet may preserve ice from the last ice age, which would make its cores the oldest recovered from the region. The findings appear in Science Advances and concern the Guliya ice cap on the Tibetan Plateau.

Cores drilled in 1992 and in 2015 showed strikingly similar oxygen isotope patterns. Lead author Lonnie Thompson says that “reproducibility of the records within a given ice cap is extremely important.” To date the ice, the researchers searched for beryllium and chlorine isotopes marking a reversal of Earth’s magnetic field more than 41,000 years ago, then matched the oxygen signals against nearby cave records.

On that basis they estimate the record may extend well beyond 128,000 years, far longer than the roughly 12,000 years once assumed. Caution is needed, however: the age is inferred from comparisons rather than measured directly, and the press material gives no margin of error. The authors, whose work was funded by the US National Science Foundation, plan to analyse further samples to refine the timeline.

questions.a: That records from within one ice cap must be reproducible.

questions.q: What did the team use to mark a point in time?
questions.a: Beryllium and chlorine isotopes linked to a reversal of Earth’s magnetic field.

questions.q: Why should the 128,000-year figure be treated carefully?
questions.a: It is inferred from comparisons, with no stated margin of error.
